record.title: Prescribed-overlap pairs near ground energy
record.locator: Proposition 1, equation (5), p.5; proof pp.15–16. Mixed-spin covariance n xi(R); the long record supplies the common-Gaussian correction for unordered-pair SK.

aligned_passages.text:
Choose one minimizer supplied by the attained Parisi formula, and apply
the full-support theorem to that same coefficient. The external landscape
theorem below then applies at every point of its Stieltjes support. For every fixed $r\in[0,1)$ and $\varepsilon,\eta>0$,
there is a constant $K=K(r,\varepsilon,\eta)>0$, independent of $n$, such that
$$
\mathbb P\left(\exists\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}^n:
\left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i\tau_i-r\right|<\varepsilon,
\quad \frac{H_n(\sigma)}n,\frac{H_n(\tau)}n\ge P_*-\eta\right)
\ge1-Ke^{-n/K},\qquad n\ge1.
$$
The probability is over the SK couplings; the configurations may depend on
them. This is the specialization of [Auffinger–Chen–Zeng, Proposition 1,
equation (5), p. 5][acz] to the full-support minimizer above. Their theorem
applies to each point of its Stieltjes support. Its proof, on pp. 15–16,
uses the coupled free energy constrained to a neighbourhood of that
overlap, passes to the coupled maximum and applies Gaussian concentration.
The coupled maximum approaches $2P_*$, while the unrestricted maximum
approaches $P_*$; these two facts force both members of a maximizing pair
to be near ground energy.

The covariance normalization needs one small adjustment. Writing
$R=n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i\tau_i$, our Hamiltonian has covariance
$nR^2/2-1/2$. Adjoin a common independent Gaussian $C$ of variance $1/2$.
Then $\widetilde H_n(\sigma)=H_n(\sigma)+C$ has covariance
$n\xi(R)$ with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, as in the cited mixed-spin theorem.
Its expected maximum equals that of $H_n$, so its ground-state limit is
the same $P_*$. Apply the theorem with energy tolerance $\eta/2$.
On $|C|\le\eta n/2$, the resulting pair also satisfies the displayed
energy inequalities for $H_n$. The omitted event has probability at most
$2e^{-\eta^2n^2/4}$, which can be absorbed into $Ke^{-n/K}$ by enlarging
$K$. Since the conclusion for $H_n$ depends only on its couplings,
this also removes the auxiliary Gaussian from the probability statement.

The pointwise result also gives a simultaneous statement at any fixed
positive resolution. Given $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, choose finitely many
centres $r_j\in[0,1)$ whose open $\varepsilon/2$-neighbourhoods cover
$[0,1]$. Apply the preceding result at each centre with overlap tolerance
$\varepsilon/2$ and energy tolerance $\eta$. A finite union bound gives
constants $C,c>0$, depending only on these tolerances, such that
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(\forall r\in[-1,1]\ \exists\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}^n:
 |R(\sigma,\tau)-r|<\varepsilon,\quad
 H_n(\sigma)/n,H_n(\tau)/n\ge P_*-\eta\right)
 \ge1-Ce^{-cn}.
\tag{9.1}
$$
Indeed, on the event where every centre has a suitable pair, choose a
nearest centre and use the triangle inequality. For negative targets,
reverse one spin configuration: the pure two-spin Hamiltonian preserves
its energy and changes the overlap's sign. The finite net covers the
endpoints as well, with centres strictly below one.

This deduction uses fixed tolerances and target-dependent pairs. It gives
neither exact arbitrary real overlaps at finite $n$, a typical-pair law,
a search procedure, nor a guarantee for tolerances shrinking with $n$.
It uses the external landscape theorem, full support and attainment, and
is outside the two selected formal statements in §12. The separate
algorithmic consequence is in §9.4.

The Sherrington–Kirkpatrick (SK) model asks us to choose signs that
maximise a random sum of pair interactions. The Parisi formula expresses
the limiting maximum through a nondecreasing function, the **order
parameter**. We explain why a minimising order parameter cannot be
constant on any interval below one.

The proof compares two consequences of a hypothetical gap. Minimality
fixes the values and bounds the slopes of an auxiliary curve at its
endpoints. An analytic estimate makes the derivative strictly convex
between them, leaving too little area to connect the required values.
Initial and terminal gaps need separate arguments. We then return to
the spins: a theorem about their energies gives nearly optimal sign
choices differing on any prescribed positive fraction of positions up to one half,
with arbitrarily small error in that fraction.

We follow the quantitative proof in [OpenAI (2026a)][support-manuscript];
[Hong-Bin Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3][chen-support] had already proved
full support by a different method. The estimate used here makes the
final contradiction a direct comparison of areas. We assume algebra
and elementary calculus, and introduce probability and cumulative mass
through calculations. The deeper analytic facts are stated where the
proof needs them. By the end of Sections 1–6, the reader should be able
to reconstruct how minimality and those inputs exclude each kind of gap,
then translate the result into a statement about spin configurations.
Section 7 gives optional calculations and answers to the short questions
in the text; the full analytic proofs remain in the cited sources.

## 6. Return to the spins We can now return to the arrangement of nearly optimal spin choices. A separate theorem of [Auffinger–Chen–Zeng, Proposition 1, equation (5)][acz] applies at each point in the minimiser's support. Combining it with full support: for every fixed overlap $r\in[0,1)$ and tolerances $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, with probability over the couplings tending to one exponentially fast as $n\to\infty$, there exist configurations $\sigma,\tau$ with $$ |R(\sigma,\tau)-r|<\varepsilon, \qquad H_n(\sigma)/n,\ H_n(\tau)/n\ge P_*-\eta. $$ If $k$ sites differ, $k/n=(1-R)/2$. The overlap tolerance therefore gives $$ \left|\frac{k}{n}-\frac{1-r}{2}\right|<\frac\varepsilon2. $$ For example, fix an energy loss $\eta>0$ per spin and take $r=1/2$ and $\varepsilon=0.02$. With probability tending to one exponentially fast, the same instance has two configurations with energies per spin at least $P_*-\eta$ and a differing-site fraction between $0.24$ and $0.26$. No numerical threshold for $n$ is asserted. At target zero, the differing-site fraction can be arbitrarily close to one half. The pair may depend on the chosen target and the couplings. This is existence for each fixed target, not a statement about typically sampled pairs or a procedure for finding them. The companion *Long Reasoning Record*, [§9.3, “Near-ground configurations at a prescribed overlap”](../long/reasoning-record.md#near-ground-overlaps), gives the probability bound and the covariance adjustment.
